title: Kennedy Center exterior remains covered after Trump’s name is removed | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

Large striped tarps remain on the Kennedy Center’s exterior, prompting confusion and frustration from some visitors who arrived to the renowned arts venue tosee President Donald Trump’s name removed.

Stephen Caken, a New York resident visiting Washington, DC, for an internship, told CNN on Sunday he was puzzled why the tarp was still up after the president’s name was removed on Saturday in compliance with a federal judge’s order.

“It seems like they’re trying to just kind of take away attention from this whole charade,” Caken said.

“The scaffolding and tarp will remain up as crews address maintenance needs of the marble and soffit panels,” a Kennedy Center spokesperson told CNN on Monday.

Much of the building’s facade where the metal letters marking Trump’s name were installed in December remain covered, preventing many from viewing what remains. John Mathew Smith, a Maryland resident who made the trip to the Kennedy Center on Sunday, argued that Trump was “trying to weaken America’s symbols.”

“To me, he’s trying to deface America’s symbols before he starts finishing defacing the country itself,” Smith said.

Tim Terpstra, a Washington resident who lives nearby, went to the center twice over the weekend, hoping that the tarps had been removed.

“It would be nice to be able to see to make sure that it is down, and no vestiges of what was up there still remain,” he said.

The removal came after an appeals court declined to pause a ruling from US District Judge Christopher Cooper that found the venue acted unlawfully when it added Trump’s name to the building,part of the president’s effortto remake the nation’s capital.

The installation of Trump’s name to the building, which honors assassinated President John F. Kennedy, struck a symbolic chord among residents who’ve cherished the center, which has long served as a cultural hub in the deep-blue city.

The centertook steps last weekto reverse the change in some places but kept the president’s name on the building as it sought to stave off compliance with Cooper’s ruling.

On Friday, crowds gathered to stake out the removal as crews began to erect scaffolding in front of the venue’s facade. Some protestors shouted chants of “Take it down,” and at one point, called the workers “heroes.”

As workers started to drape the tarps around the scaffolding early Saturday morning, people in the crowd below chanted, “Shame!” A little after 3 a.m., workers appeared to be removing letters, according to video shot through a small opening in the scaffolding.

While the Kennedy Center’s appeal is expected to play out in coming weeks, the legal fight dates to December, when Trump’s handpicked board of trusteesadded his name, leading to a wave of artists pulling out of performances.

Rep. Joyce Beatty, an Ohio Democrat and an ex-officio trustee of the board, quicklylaunched a legal challengeagainst the name change. On Saturday, Beatty posted a celebratory video on social media of herself doinga dance popularizedby Trump to “YMCA” by The Village People.

In Trump’s second term, the venue has served as a vehicle for him to elevate work that aligns with his cultural preferences. He hosted theKennedy Center Honorsin December, and the center hosted thepremiereof first lady Melania Trump’s documentary. And last week, the center hosted the final round of Trump’snational civics contestfor high school students.

In hiseffort to reshapeWashington, DC, Trump has also paved over the White House Rose Garden to create a Mar-a-Lago-esque patio, demolished the East Wing to make room for a massive ballroom, and changed the color of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

He’s launched efforts to build a golf course, construct the tallest arch in the world on a traffic circle across from Arlington National Cemetery, and put a sculpture garden along the Potomac River.

Meanwhile, some efforts have focused more on ideology than aesthetics: White House officials have mounted a review of theSmithsonian Institutionin an effort to align the organization with the president’s views on American history and culture.

This story has been updated with additional developments.

CNN’s Devan Cole, Betsy Klein and Kaanita Iyer contributed to this report.

CNN’s Devan Cole, Betsy Klein and Kaanita Iyer contributed to this report.
